story.title: Monsoon rains swell the rivers
story.lead: Heavy downpours across Jakarta caused rivers to swell and overflow their banks [1]. Emergency teams responded quickly to protect homes [2].
story.image_caption: Monsoon rain clouds over Southeast Asia seen from space

story.body_1: When severe rainfall hits Jakarta, storm water rushes into local rivers [1]. As water levels rise rapidly, the weight of the water creates intense pressure against walls and embankments [2]. Satellites track these weather patterns across Southeast Asia during the monsoon season [3].
story.body_2: Understanding water pressure helps engineers build stronger dikes and flood defenses [2]. Even a small increase in water depth adds significant force against barriers [1].
timeline.2.text: River water levels rise and put pressure on embankments [2].
physics.title: Hydrostatic pressure
physics.body_1: Water has weight. The deeper you go in a pool or a swollen river, the more water is piled up above you. This creates hydrostatic pressure.
physics.body_2: Hydrostatic pressure depends on three things: the density of the water (ρ), gravity (g), and the depth or height of the water column (h).
physics.assumptions: We assume water density is constant and ignore atmospheric pressure for the net fluid pressure.
table.note: Pressure grows in direct step with depth.

physics.tip: Double the depth, double the pressure! Water pushes outward in all directions, not just downward.

lab.title: Bottle pressure test
lab.step_1: Poke three small holes at different heights down the side of a plastic bottle.
lab.step_2: Cover holes with tape, fill bottle with water, and place in a basin.
lab.step_3: Remove the tape and observe how far the water squirts from each hole.
lab.question: Which hole squirted water the furthest? Use pressure and depth to explain why.
